chapter_theme: Akananuru 41 to 60, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men away for wealth and women and mothers left behind, set beside hill courtships moving toward disclosure and marriage, marutham quarrels over the husband's other women, mullai homecomings and neythal pleas. Puram names (Venni, Musiri, Kurukkai, Pazhaiyan, Pannan) are used throughout as similes for private grief and joy.

41.reading: Away on his errand for wealth, the man looks at a dawn countryside in full beauty, the palasa ablaze with flowers, bees humming and ploughmen calling over the fields, and asks whether the dark-skinned, freckled woman he left is wasting, her shoulders slackening, in the loneliness of his absence.
41.nuance: The landscape gains its beauty (காடுஅணி கொண்ட) in the very lines where she loses hers (நலம் செலச் சாஅய்); the season that adorns the land is the measure of what parting takes from her, and he can only guess it with a question (கொல்லோ).

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த விடத்துக் கிழத்தியை நினைந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man speaks from inside a parting he chose; the fields around him are marutham

comparisons.tenor: the palasa's flowering branches, as fire
the fine freckles on her dark skin, like pollen spray on tender leaves

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named: he speaks his thought aloud

42.reading: The friend tells the heroine that the joy of a whole people when heavy rain at dawn fills a dried-out tank after a long drought has all been poured into her, because the lord of the sky-touching hills has come.
42.nuance: The friend speaks of her own joy, not the heroine's; the drought image measures how long the waiting for marriage had become, and the whole land rejoicing hints that the marriage will be public, the opposite of secret love.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் வரைவு மலிந்தமை தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord's coming to marry decides it; the drought and tank belong to the simile

comparisons.tenor: the red-cornered eyes, against the red back of jasmine buds
her body, like tender leaves
the tank's high banks, like hills

comparisons.vehicle: பல்லோர் உவந்த உவகை எல்லாம் என்னுள் பெய்தந் தற்று
comparisons.tenor: the friend's joy at the hill lord's coming, like the people's joy at rain after drought

43.reading: The man tells the heart that urged him to go for wealth that the monsoon has come, the clouds joining land and sky so that only water-clock keepers know where the sun is, and he has held his mullai-scented wife; pitiable are those who, without kindness, leave their sweet companion for a stranger's wealth.
43.nuance: He calls the wealth-seeker's departure மடமை, folly, the word usually kept for the woman's innocence; the cow elephant, worn by summer and now bathing with her bull in the flood, is the rains' gift to the paired, and he places himself with the pair.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்கடைக் கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the situation is a refused departure for wealth; the land and season are mullai's

iraicchi.act: the cow elephant, worn by the summer heat, goes into the flood to bathe together with her bull
iraicchi.sense: the rains bring the parted together, and the man who has stayed to hold his wife is doing what the elephants do

44.reading: The king's war is done and the enemy has paid tribute, so the man bids his charioteer drive ahead of the column, that he may sleep on the breast of a wife who is like Kudavayil, a town as rich as Chenni's Azhumbil; Chenni is the king who, unable to bear the sight of Pazhaiyan's fall, when the chiefs Nannan, Etrai, Atti, Kangan, Katti and Punthurai had massed their camp, captured Kanaiyan and took Kazhumalam.
44.nuance: The catalogue of chiefs and the fall of Pazhaiyan fill lines 7 to 17, and the wife is reached only through a chain of likenesses, a king, his town, another town; the war that kept him away is also the stock from which he praises her. Who fought whom in lines 7 to 14 is compressed, and this reading of it is offered with caution.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man returns from finished work to the waiting wife

comparisons.tenor: Kudavayil's unfailing wealth, like Chenni's Azhumbil
the wife, like the cool, rich town of Kudavayil

45.reading: Told to bear up, the heroine says her lover has crossed a summer forest where dry pods rattle like dancing-floor drums and the tiger springs on the waterless track; her skin must pale like peerkku flowers, the gossip is louder than the bards' clamour the day Anni cut down Thithiyan's punnai at Kurukkai, and she will wander distraught like Aathimanthi, sleepless as a broken fort shaken by the Chera's assault.
45.nuance: Every likeness she reaches for is a public disaster: a battlefield's din, a famous madwoman, a sacked fort. Her private loss is told in the scale of puram events, which is how she answers the friend's claim that it can be borne.

colophon.thurai: வற்புறுக்குந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover has gone through the forest and she cannot bear it

comparisons.tenor: the rattling of dry uzhinjil pods, like the dancing-floor drum
her pallor, like the peerkku flower
the gossip, louder than the bards' clamour at Kurukkai
her distracted wandering, like Aathimanthi's
her sleepless dread, like a broken-walled fort under assault

46.reading: The friend refuses the man entry: he is lord of a town where a red-eyed buffalo, tired of the mud, breaks its tether in the sleeping night, pushes through the thorn fence, scatters the fish and grazes the lotus; they say he has brought another woman home and married her, and the friend will not say it herself, but her bangle, like Chezhiyan's Allur, may slip if it must; go, lord, who is stopping you?
46.nuance: The refusal is made as a release: யாரையோ நிற் புலக்கேம் (who are we to quarrel with you) and நிற் றகைக்குநர் யாரோ (who is there to stop you) deny her any claim on him, which is the sharpest claim she can make. The report of the wedding is put in others' mouths (என்ப).

colophon.thurai: வாயில் வேண்டிச் சென்ற தலைமகற்குத் தோழி வாயின் மறுத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's side quarrels with a husband who has taken another woman

comparisons.tenor: the husband who breaks the household's bond for a new woman
the speaker's bright bangle, rich and fine as Chezhiyan's town Allur

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the new wife he has brought home

pairs.situation: he breaks the bond of his household
he does it secretly, while the town sleeps
the household is thrown into disorder

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a buffalo of the marutham fields in a marutham poem, without leaving the land (porul 7.27)

47.reading: The man tells his faltering heart to rise quickly now the work is done, cross the hot wilderness where wind-whipped bamboo catches fire, the flames leap the crags and cracking joints scatter the stags, and at dusk, when lamps are lit and the male dove calls its mate in the tall house, reach her who weeps asking where he is, and embrace many times her bamboo-smooth shoulders, fragrant with the koothalam of Chezhiyan's Sirumalai.
47.nuance: He pictures the dusk at home before he has crossed the fire: the lamps, the calling dove and her question 'யாண்டு உளர்கொல்?' are what make the burning road crossable.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்து அழிந்த நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot wilderness to be crossed on the way home

comparisons.tenor: her rounded shoulders, like bamboo

iraicchi.act: at lamp-lighting the red-legged male dove calls to its beloved mate in the tall house
iraicchi.sense: at the hour when even the dove calls its mate home, the husband's absence is felt most, and his return is owed

48.reading: The friend answers the foster mother, who asks why her daughter will not drink milk and has paled: when the girls went to pick vengai flowers and someone cried 'tiger', a garlanded young hunter came asking which way the beast went, asked if such girls could lie, gazed long at her daughter's eyes and drove away, and at sunset the daughter looked where he had gone and said 'he is a man indeed'; the wise can measure the rest.
48.nuance: The friend never names love. She gives the scene and the daughter's one sentence and leaves the inference to the foster mother (மதிவல் லோர்க்கே), a disclosure that keeps the girl's modesty. His question about lies plays on their silence: they hid and did not answer where the beast went.

colophon.thurai: செவிலித்தாய்க்குத் தோழி அறத்தொடு நின்றது.

thinai_evidence.note: a first meeting with the hill lord on the slope

comparisons.tenor: the red water-lily petals of his garland, like eyes

49.reading: The foster mother grieves at home: she had seen the girl who loved her parrot, ball and play-seeds grow unlike herself, had come close, stroked her forehead and held her, and the girl had embraced her again and again; had she known the girl would go, praising the tall man, through a forest where tired deer chew withered marul in the rainless shade, she would have followed her like her own shadow wherever she played in her father's house.
49.nuance: Her regret is not that she failed to stop the girl but that she was not near enough: the shadow image (மெய்ந்நிழல் போல) makes her wish to have gone along. The girl's many embraces, read now, were a farewell the mother did not understand.

colophon.thurai: உடன் போயின தலைமகளை நினைந்து செவிலித்தாய் மனையின்கண் வருந்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has gone with her lover through the forest

comparisons.tenor: the foster mother watching the girl's back, like a cow tied with its calf
the foster mother following the girl everywhere, like the body's shadow

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: she grieves alone at home; no hearer is named

50.reading: The friend tells the bard that the shore lord once came often, even by day, despite the leaping fish of the backwater and the red-mouthed women's gossip, and now stays away; she asks him to go secretly to the old town and tell the hero what the bright-browed girl says as she hides her tears: 'see, the anril on the palmyra by the house cannot sleep at night if parted from its mate even once; what shall I do?'
50.nuance: The anril is the girl's own message, not an image the poem lodges: she uses the bird to say that she cannot sleep, so it carries the sense openly rather than as iraicchi. The friend, not the girl, chooses the bard as carrier, and asks him to go secretly.

colophon.thurai: தோழி பாணனுக்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater and the shore lord

51.reading: The man tells his heart, which urged him to leave, that in the peopleless summer wilderness where a male vulture with flesh-red ears sits scorched on a burnt yaa tree gazing at its hungry mate, the wealth he would toil for is not worth having if it comes only by parting from his wife: better to stay, hold her close so her jewels jingle, and be glad in the household's work.
51.nuance: The hinge is the play on புணர்வு: wealth is 'joined' only by parting, and staying is the other joining, with her. The vulture stays by its mate in the burning tree; the hearth (மனைமுதல் வினை) is set against the work (செய்வினை) abroad.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் கடைக்கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer wilderness he refuses to cross

comparisons.tenor: the vulture's red ears, like flesh stuck on

iraicchi.act: the male vulture, its wings scorched, stays on the burning tree looking at the face of its hungry mate
iraicchi.sense: even the vulture in the fire does not leave its mate, which is the choice the man makes against his heart

52.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the two-sided question, whether to tell mother of the hill lord whose wide chest their heart loves, a lord of a land where a girl's cry for vengai flowers brings the men running with bows for a cattle-seizing tiger, has been settled one way: even if her life leaves her body, the friend must not say that her pallor is love-sickness.
52.nuance: The colophon says she speaks knowing the friend will disclose; her forbidding is modesty speaking, and the oath (இன்உயிர் கழிவது ஆயினும்) shows the cost she sets on silence. The false alarm on the hill, a girl's cry taken for a tiger's threat, is how secrets get out in this land.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் வேறுபட்டமையறிந்த செவிலித்தாய்க்குத் தோழி அறத்தொடு நிற்குமெனத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope and the hill lord

comparisons.tenor: the new vengai flowers, like gold

53.reading: The heroine tells the friend who urges patience that she does not know: he has crossed the waterless wilderness of drumstick flowers and cactus, where a red dog rests with its starving mate in the shade of a lettered hero-stone, because his heart cannot hide what it has when the needy say they have nothing; his love is for wealth more than for her, and the friend calls it grace.
53.nuance: She grants him the virtue and turns it against her: the inability to refuse the poor is what takes him away, so his generosity and his desertion are the same act. The last two lines set காதல் against காதல் and பொருள் against அருள்.

colophon.thurai: வற்புறுக்குந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless wilderness he crossed

iraicchi.act: the red dog, itself hungry, keeps with its starving mate and rests beside her in the hero-stone's shade
iraicchi.sense: even the wild dog of that waste stays with its hungry mate, while the man has left his for wealth

54.reading: The guest kings have paid tribute and the king's anger has cooled, the rains have come, so the man bids his charioteer drive over the red earth that the cochineal beetles make like a painting: at dusk, when the cattle hurry home to their calves with the cowherds behind, he wants to see his wife beckon the young moon with her finger, prattling sweet as water after gooseberries from the garden of Pannan, who lives for others, promising it milk if it brings their son a gold tali.
54.nuance: What he hurries home to is not her waiting but her play: the mother tricking the child with the moon (புதல்வற் பொய்க்கும்). The village whose gooseberry gives the simile is that of Pannan, praised in one line as தனக்கென வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன், a puram patron lodged inside an akam homecoming.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுடித்து மீளும் தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains, the evening and the cowherds driving cattle home

comparisons.tenor: the red earth strewn with velvet mites, like a painting
her sweet prattle, like water to one who has eaten green gooseberry

iraicchi.act: at dusk the milch cows, udders full, hurry lowing to the homes where their tethered calves wait
iraicchi.sense: the man's return at the same hour is the cattle's return to their young: he goes home to his wife and son

55.reading: The mother tells the neighbour women who console her that she does not grieve that her daughter went with a youth strong as an elephant across the sun-cracked waste; she lies sleepless, breathing hot like a forge's bellows, and quarrels with her own life, which will not leave her to go after the girl as the noble men who heard Cheralathan, shamed by his back wound at Venni, sit facing north, died to go with him.
55.nuance: She accepts the match (கழிந்ததற்கு அழிந்தன்றோ இலனே) and turns her anger on her own life for staying. The puram image is chosen for its followers, not its king: the companions who chose death with him are what her life refuses to be.

colophon.thurai: புணர்ந்துடன் போன தலமகட்கு இரங்கிய தாய் தெருட்டும் அயலிலாட்டியர்க்கு உரைத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has gone with her lover across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the youth, strong as an elephant
her hot inward breathing, like a forge's bellows
her heart, as if burning

comparisons.vehicle: சான்றோர் அரும்பெறல் உலகத்து அவனொடு செலீஇயர் பெரும்பிறிது ஆகி யாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: her life, which will not follow her daughter as the noble men followed their king into death

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: the addressees are the neighbour women who console her

56.reading: The heroine laughs to her friend that yesterday the bard of the lord of the cool ford, where a black-horned buffalo stirs the gem-clear pond, gorges on lilies and comes home dusted with kaanji pollen, was hurrying to bring new brides to the lord's chest when a newly calved cow charged him; he dropped his lute and ran into her house, and when she hid her mirth and said 'this is not your house, that one is', he stood bewildered with folded hands.
56.nuance: The laugh is the weapon: by sending the bard to 'your house' she names the courtesan's house as his true home and her husband's errand-runner as a stranger in hers. The joy she hides (மெய்ம்மலி உவகை மறையினென்) is a joy in his discomfiture.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தைமனைக்குச் செல்கின்ற பாணன் தன் மனைக்கு *வந்தசனாகத் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's new women and the bard who serves them

comparisons.tenor: the clear pond, like a gem
the buffalo's black horns, like wrought iron
the husband who takes many new women and comes home marked by them

ullurai.tenor: the husband and his new brides

pairs.situation: he comes home bearing their marks

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the buffalo at the pond of her own town, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

57.reading: On the summer road among the hills, where a small green-feathered female bird crosses the sky in the heat, finds no fruit on the bare fig whose roots hang like an elephant's trunk, and faints remembering the days of plenty, the man, alone, wonders whether his wife's beauty, bright as the full moon, has turned to the colour of peerkku flowers, as she weeps night and day like the wounded in Chezhiyan's siege of Musiri.
57.nuance: The bird comes to a tree that once fed it and finds it empty, as the man imagines his wife finding the days of their life together gone; the war simile of the wounded at Musiri makes her grief a casualty of the same world of kings and wealth that took him away.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் வயிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் கிழத்தியை நினைந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the long summer road

comparisons.tenor: the fig's hanging roots, like an elephant's raised trunk
her beauty, like the full moon
her paled colour, like peerkku flowers
her suffering, like that of the gravely wounded at Musiri

iraicchi.act: the female bird comes back to the fig that once fed her, finds no fruit, and wilts remembering the days of plenty
iraicchi.sense: the wife, left alone, remembers the full days together and finds them gone

58.reading: The heroine tells the hill lord, whose land is one where at midnight in cold-season rain the hunter father of the hill girls, finding no game, keeps to his house on a tiger-skin bed, that it is sweet when her arms clasp his back on his chest; but the cold north wind, which torments her whenever she thinks of him in his absence, waits long outside at midnight, bending the house tree, looking for its chance.
58.nuance: The father kept home by the rain is the danger to their meeting, and the wind that waits outside is like the lover who stood outside; the close of the poem (நெடும்புற நிலையே) may be his long waiting or the wind's, and the reading turns on which.

colophon.thurai: சேட்படுத்து வந்த தலைமகற்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord and the midnight of the cold season

59.reading: The friend tells the heroine, whose eyes have lost their flower-like beauty, that on the road taken by the man who went far for wealth a bull elephant bends a tall yaa tree with his head so his young mate can eat its shoots, as Maal trod down a tree on the Yamuna's sands to give the cowherd girls leaf-skirts; yet those men do not remember even the mornings when they praised her back, lovely as the water-lily of Murugan's Parankunram, and have left her shoulders to slacken.
59.nuance: The comfort is double: the elephant who feeds his mate is meant to promise the man's return, while the friend also admits he does not think of her. The god's image of a tree bent for women's sake makes the elephant's care a divine habit.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட கிழத்திக்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left for wealth in a far land

comparisons.tenor: the bull elephant bending the yaa tree for his mate, like Maal treading down a tree for the cowherd girls

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant bends the tall yaa tree with his head so that his young mate can eat its shoots, and fans the bees from his cheek
iraicchi.sense: on the very road the man took, the male feeds his mate, so he too will remember and come back to care for her

60.reading: The friend tells the hero: do not crush our bright bangle, fine as Porayan's Tondi where a fisher girl brings her father rice bartered for salt, tamarind fish stew and fat fish; if the mother, who flushes at nothing and says 'playing in the sand with your friends wears away your glow', sees anything, she will shut the girl in more closely than the Chola guards the tribute stored at Kudanthai.
60.nuance: The threat of confinement is the argument for marriage: the friend never asks him to marry but makes the mother's guarded house the alternative. The fisher girl feeding her father in the opening is the life of the shore the heroine is about to lose.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்குத் தோழி செறிப்பறிவுறீஇ வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea, the fishing boats and the shore

comparisons.tenor: the heroine's bright bangle, rich and fine as Porayan's Tondi
the mother's confinement of the girl, closer than the Chola's guarded tribute at Kudanthai

links.note: Both liken the beloved's coming to rain on those who live by it: the Kural states it as a rule of lovers' grace, Akananuru 42 makes it a drought broken at dawn over a whole countryside.
links.teaches: The Kural's two-line rain simile is the compressed form of a scene the Sangam poet builds at length, so the couplet's image carries the whole drought-and-tank picture behind it.

links.note: In 43 the man calls leaving a companion for wealth folly (மடமை) and pities those who do it; in 53 the heroine says her man left because his heart could not refuse the needy, a virtue she still reads as love of wealth over her.
links.teaches: Read together they show the paalai debate from both sides: the same departure is folly to one man and an unrefusable duty of giving to another, and the woman left behind refuses to call either grace.

links.note: Kural 1268 says let the king fight and win, and let us feast at home in the evening; Akananuru 44 opens with the king's work done and the tribute paid, and bids the chariot race home to sleep on her breast.
links.teaches: The Kural's couplet is the akam homecoming formula of the returning warrior reduced to its two clauses, the king's victory first and the household's evening second.

links.note: Akananuru 44 records Pazhaiyan's fall in a war of many chiefs; Akananuru 186 uses Pazhaiyan's town Por on the Kaveri as a likeness for a bangle that will not be broken.
links.teaches: The same chief appears in one akam poem as a fallen man and in another as the owner of an unbreakable town, so akam poets drew on a chief's fame both before and after his fall.

links.note: Both use Anni's cutting of Thithiyan's punnai at Kurukkai: 45 measures the gossip by the bards' clamour that day, 145 wishes on the foster mother's hand the fate of that felled tree.
links.teaches: One puram event served akam poets in two opposite ways, as a measure of noise and as a curse of destruction, which shows these battles were a shared stock of reference the audience was expected to know.

links.note: Both have the wife's side refuse the husband who has been with other women: the Kural's woman will not touch the chest other women's eyes have fed on, the friend of 46 refuses him the door and says 'go, who stops you'.
links.teaches: The Kural compresses into one refusal what the Sangam poem makes a situation with a hidden buffalo image, a report of a new marriage and a mocking release, so the couplet is the end point of a whole marutham scene.

links.note: Both liken a woman's bangle to a rich king's town (Chezhiyan's Allur in 46, Pazhaiyan's Por in 186), one from the wife's side and one from the courtesan's.
links.teaches: The town-like bangle is a shared formula that both rivals in the marutham triangle could use, so the formula marks a woman's claim on the man, not which side she is on.

links.note: In both a cry of 'tiger' on the vengai slope brings men running: in 48 the girls' cry brings the young hunter who becomes the lover, in 52 a hill girl's cry for flowers brings the hill men with bows.
links.teaches: Together they show the vengai-plucking cry as a known custom of the hill, and 48 turns that public alarm into the private occasion of a first meeting that 52's heroine now wants kept secret.

links.note: Kural 1155 says if he leaves, union becomes hard (நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு); in 51 the man tells his heart that wealth is joined only by parting, and chooses to stay.
links.teaches: The same word புணர்வு carries both sides of one exchange: the Kural's woman counts what parting costs union, and the Sangam man counts what union costs wealth.

links.note: Kural 1138 says love breaks through secrecy into the public square whatever the lover's restraint; in 52 the heroine, her pallor already visible, still forbids her friend to name it even at the cost of her life.
links.teaches: The Kural's rule that love cannot be hidden is qualified by the Sangam heroine's will: the body discloses it, but the naming is still hers to refuse.

links.note: Kural 223 counts not saying 'I have nothing' and giving as the mark of the well-born; in 53 that very inability to refuse the needy is what drives the man away from the heroine.
links.teaches: The Kural's praise of giving has a cost the Kural does not count: in akam the generous man's virtue is the cause of the woman's abandonment.

links.note: Pannan of Sirukudi is praised in Purananuru 173 as the healer of hunger whose house feeds crowds; in Akananuru 54 his village's gooseberry gives the simile and he is called one who lives not for himself but for others.
links.teaches: An akam poet could fold a puram patron's reputation into one epithet inside a love poem, which shows how well-known Pannan's generosity was.

links.note: Purananuru 182 says the world stands because there are those who strive not for themselves but for others (தமக்கென முயலா ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்); Akananuru 54 calls Pannan தனக்கென வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன்.
links.teaches: The kaanchi poem's general ideal and the akam poem's praise of one patron use the same contrast of self and others, so the maxim was already a phrase of praise for real patrons.

links.note: Both tell of Cheralathan, ashamed of his back wound from the fight with Karikalan, sitting facing north to die; Purananuru 65 laments the king, Akananuru 55 turns to the noble men who died with him.
links.teaches: The akam poem keeps a detail the puram lament leaves out, the companions who followed the king into death, and uses it to measure a mother's wish that her life would follow her daughter.

links.note: Both use the battle at Venni: in 246 the uproar of Karikalan's victory measures the town's gossip, in 55 the defeated Chera's death measures a mother's grief.
links.teaches: One battle gave akam poets images from both sides, the victor's clamour for gossip and the loser's death for grief, so a puram event's meaning in akam depends on whose side the image is taken from.

links.note: Both name Chezhiyan's attack on Musiri, the Chera port: 149 has him seize an image there, 57 compares the wife's suffering to the wounded in that clamorous siege.
links.teaches: Two separate paalai poems witness the same Pandya assault on Musiri, which shows a single war entering the akam repertoire as a ready image of suffering and plunder.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage: the formal union that ends secret love, sought or pressed for in the akam poems
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons' word (வரைவு மலிந்தமை, வரைவு கடாயது)

source_issues: 44: the colophon thinai is the numbering rule's முல்லை; the commentary edition gives பாலை. The poem (a man returning from finished war to his wife) fits mullai.
47: the base text numbers the last line 15 though the poem has 19 lines, as the commentary edition shows; a misprinted number.
55: the colophon thurai reads தலமகட்கு, a misprint for தலைமகட்கு.
56: the colophon thurai has the corrupt word *வந்தசனாக, presumably வந்தானாக (the bard came to her house).
57: the base text has 19 lines and the commentary edition (pmuni0490_01) 18; marked as the base text stands.
